children.text: What are the minimum Mac requirements?

Hey HN,

I’m building BetterWispr, a free and open-source voice dictation app for macOS.

I wanted to make voice typing more accessible without requiring a monthly subscription or sending every recording to a cloud server.

You can hold Option + Space, speak naturally, and have the transcription inserted directly into whatever app you’re using.

A few things I’ve been working on:

- Local speech recognition using Whisper, Parakeet, or Apple Speech - Automatic cleanup of filler words and repeated phrases - Custom vocabulary for names and technical terms - Different writing styles depending on the app - Optional meeting transcription and summaries

The project is open source under Apache 2.0.

I’m still improving the experience, especially around transcription accuracy, speed, and reliability across different Macs.

I’d love feedback from people who regularly use voice dictation.

What would make you switch from your current dictation tool to an open-source alternative?

Website: https://betterwispr.com/

children.text: Qwen 3.8 Flash Next also works very well with this, and frankly even the much smaller 3.6 35B-A3B did, too.

So this is the actual amazing thing. Claude does absolutely fantastic with rambling. As I am dictating I may change my mind three times as I keep imagining new cases or new constraints. And then at the end of my prompt I will say something like OK this has been a whole lot of brainstorming in different directions. I'd like you to summarize from me what you interpret as the final decisions and the reasoning behind it and the reasoning for why we are not going to adopt the proposed alternatives. And then tell me if you think I'm missing anything.

And it does. I don't even have to write out my final thoughts neatly summarized myself. Claude figures it out on its own and saves me a bunch of time. It's much faster for me to read it's logically laid out conclusions and confirm that that is actually what I had meant. Never once have I seen it get it wrong, but quite frequently it raises additional points for me to consider or highlights potential inconsistencies in what I have said.

So the actual session itself with Claude includes a whole lot of rambling and brainstorming, but then the actual documented artifacts of the session are the nice clean summary of what we figured out. And then, for example, when we move from a brainstorming design phase into a coding implementation phase, I'll start a brand new session so that it's context isn't polluted by the brainstorming and rambling but is rather starting off with the nicely organized document that had been created as the artifact from the previous session.

And this is why dictation works so well as a feature. Because it means I frequently wind up essentially "oversharing" my product requirements with Claude, and it will frequently suggest potential solutions that I had overlooked because I was already assuming that the solution would take a particular form. So it becomes surprisingly collaborative rather than me just dumping requirements into Claude.

How do you keep your prompts from getting just ramblings as you do the thinking?

It sounds like a fun way to "code", but I just can't imagine how it works in reality.

children.author: zalthor
children.text:
Interestingly enough, I was working on something very similar this past few of days[1]! A couple of things that I did differently -

One, in the post-transcription cleanup phase, instead of programmatically fixing the text, I just feed the text with a prompt + dictionary of words into an LLM. Initially tried doing this with the on-device model from Apple in macOS 27, but that was too slow. I've now been playing around with gpt-oss-20b on Groq, which appears to be fast and effective. Although I'm curious how well your programmatic approach works, I might try some sort of a bake off over the next few days. But in the long run, I think I might still stick with an LLM-based formatter because you can have far more interesting formatting considerations or formatting prompts based on the app that you are using or the style or tone of your dictated text.

Two - When building the dictionary of words to fix, I'm also including a recording of the word and having the transcription model just predict draft out variants to use as replacements.

[1] https://github.com/goose42/TalkToMyMac

Spot on. My backup local notetaker app just stopped releasing updates and became broken so I got annoyed and just whipped up my own to not lose access to my old recordings and also to just use going forward.

So much better to just add my own features and slowly customize it to suit my needs.

I have a fun feature where I can retranscribe with multiple local models and then compare transcripts and optionally label/correct them to accumulate data on which models are most accurate over time.

On MacOS, dictation was solved a while back with Parakeet V3, and I haven't seen anything that has a better speed/accuracy tradeoff when talking to AIs, where slight inaccuracies are ok since they can "read between the lines".

I got annoyed by various UI and other things in tools like VoiceInk, Handy etc and Claude-Coded my own CLI dictation tool called VoxType that uses parakeet-mlx:

https://pchalasani.github.io/claude-code-tools/tools/voxtype...

Install this skill for your coding agent and let it help you set it up, there are many config options:

    npx skills add pchalasani/claude-code-tools -s voxtype-install -g
Or if you must do it yourself,

    uv tool install voxtype
This is just an example of where we are today with software today: people building their own tools, and not bothering to market it (or perhaps I'm contracting myself here ;).
